qs.q: Which process describes the action of Joseph Lister in the history of medical microbiology?
o: Formulating the fundamental postulates for infectious disease causality
Isolating the specific bacterium responsible for causing human tuberculosis
Pioneering antiseptic surgery using carbolic acid on instruments and wounds
Disproving spontaneous generation and introducing pasteurization processes
qs.e: Joseph Lister pioneered antiseptic surgery by utilizing carbolic acid to sterilize wounds and surgical instruments, validating germ theory clinically. Robert Koch isolated Mycobacterium tuberculosis and created postulates for disease causality.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Clinically oriented guide to common infections in East Africa, focusing on bedside history, examination, pragmatic diagnostics and empiric therapy when advanced tests are unavailable.

sections.p: Microbiology is the science of microorganisms that cause disease. In low‑resource hospitals, clinicians must rely on clinical clues and simple tests to identify pathogens and guide treatment.
b: Microbes: bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites
Infection routes: contact, vector, food, water
Key principle: treat the likely pathogen while awaiting confirmation

sections.p: Microorganisms are classified by shape, Gram stain, oxygen requirement and virulence factors. These features help narrow differential diagnoses.
b: Gram‑positive cocci: staphylococci, streptococci
Gram‑negative rods: enterobacteriaceae, pseudomonas
Spore‑forming bacilli: clostridia
Virulence: toxins, capsules, adhesins

sections.p: Understanding how a pathogen spreads informs prevention and control measures on the ward.
b: Direct contact: skin, mucosa
Indirect contact: fomites, contaminated water
Vector‑borne: mosquitoes, flies
Life cycle: environmental reservoir, host infection, shedding

sections.p: Common infections in East Africa include bacterial meningitis, typhoid fever, malaria, schistosomiasis, and HIV‑associated opportunistic infections.
b: Bacterial meningitis: sudden fever, neck stiffness, altered consciousness
Typhoid: prolonged fever, abdominal pain, rose spots
Malaria: cyclical fever, anemia, splenomegaly
Schistosomiasis: hematuria, hepatosplenomegaly
HIV OIs: candidiasis, PCP, tuberculosis

sections.p: When sophisticated labs are absent, use rapid tests, simple microscopy and clinical scoring systems.
b: Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs): malaria, HIV, dengue
Microscopy: stool ova & parasites, sputum Gram stain
Clinical criteria: WHO meningitis case definition, typhoid score

t.b: Positive = treat with artemisinin‑based combination; negative but high suspicion → repeat test or microscopy
Positive supports empiric ceftriaxone; consider repeat if low titer
Positive → start empiric ceftriaxone + vancomycin; negative but high suspicion → lumbar puncture if safe

sections.p: Empiric therapy targets the most likely organisms while awaiting confirmation. Supportive care and infection control are essential.
b: Empiric antibiotics: ceftriaxone + vancomycin for meningitis; ceftriaxone for typhoid; artemisinin for malaria; fluconazole for fungal OIs
Avoid nephrotoxic drugs in renal impairment
Hand hygiene, barrier precautions, vector control

t.b: Chosen for broad coverage and low resistance in many settings
Avoid if no MRSA risk; monitor renal function

sections.p: Examiners test clinical reasoning, not rote memory. Focus on history, examination, differential, investigations and empiric treatment.
b: Ask about fever pattern, travel, exposure to animals, water source
Look for Kernig/Brudzinski signs in meningitis
Use WHO meningitis case definition to decide lumbar puncture
Remember malaria RDTs are cheap and rapid

sections.p: Several conditions mimic common infections; distinguishing features are key.
b: Bacterial meningitis vs viral meningitis: CSF neutrophils vs lymphocytes
Typhoid vs enteric fever: rose spots, abdominal pain
Malaria vs dengue: thrombocytopenia, rash

sections.p: Low sensitivity of tests and atypical presentations can delay diagnosis.
b: Malaria RDT false negative in low parasitemia
Widal false positive in endemic areas
CSF glucose low in bacterial but also in TB meningitis

sections.p: Urgent referral needed for life‑threatening infections.
b: Severe sepsis with hypotension
Uncontrolled bleeding
Neurological deterioration in meningitis

faq.q: What is the first step in suspected bacterial meningitis?
faq.a: Obtain a lumbar puncture if no contraindication and start empiric ceftriaxone + vancomycin immediately.

faq.q: How do you treat uncomplicated malaria in a patient with renal impairment?
faq.a: Use artemisinin‑based combination therapy; avoid quinine due to nephrotoxicity.

faq.q: When is a negative malaria RDT still concerning?
faq.a: If clinical suspicion is high (cyclical fever, splenomegaly) repeat test or do microscopy.

exam: What investigations would you order for a patient with suspected bacterial meningitis and why? — CSF Gram stain (detects bacteria), CSF opening pressure (high in meningitis), CSF cell count (neutrophilic predominance).

A 5‑year‑old presents with fever, rash, and abdominal pain. What is the most likely diagnosis and first treatment? — Typhoid fever; start ceftriaxone empirically while awaiting Widal or blood culture.

You have a patient with cyclical fever and splenomegaly. Malaria RDT is negative. What is your next step? — Repeat RDT or perform microscopy; consider other causes like dengue or malaria with low parasitemia.
Why is vancomycin added to ceftriaxone in empiric meningitis therapy? — To cover MRSA and resistant streptococci until culture results guide de‑escalation.

A patient with HIV presents with fever and weight loss. Which opportunistic infection should you consider first and why? — Tuberculosis; high prevalence, high mortality, treat with RIPE regimen after sputum confirmation.
You are in a ward with limited lab access. How would you diagnose typhoid fever? — Use Widal titer ≥1:160 as supportive evidence, but confirm with blood culture if possible.
What is the main reason to avoid quinine in malaria treatment in low‑resource settings? — Nephrotoxicity and need for monitoring, better alternatives exist.
